proposal.title: Moby Dick; or The Whale
proposal.gist: Ishmael joins the whaling ship Pequod, whose captain Ahab is driven by monomaniacal vengeance to hunt the white whale that maimed him, a quest that destroys the ship and all but one man.
proposal.question: The white whale Moby Dick — can one man's obsessive war against an indifferent, inscrutable nature ever end in anything but ruin? (a tragedy in three acts: embarkation, pursuit, destruction)

children.title: Paperwork and front matter
children.gist: Gutenberg edition notices, subtitle/byline, transcriber's notes, and the table of contents.

children.title: Title, header, and transcriber's notes
children.gist: Publisher's and transcriber's front matter identifying the edition and its textual sources.

children.title: Table of Contents
children.gist: A full chapter listing for the novel.

children.title: Loomings
children.gist: Ishmael explains his recurring urge to go to sea as a common sailor whenever he grows restless or melancholy ashore.
children.question: Why does Ishmael go to sea — what need does the ocean answer that land cannot? (a personal meditation)

children.title: Call me Ishmael
children.gist: Ishmael introduces himself and explains that going to sea is his substitute for suicide whenever he feels grim and spleen-ridden ashore.

children.title: Water-gazers of Manhattan
children.gist: He observes crowds of landsmen in the city irresistibly drawn to stare at the water, suggesting a universal human fascination with the sea.

children.title: The ungraspable phantom of life
children.gist: Meditating on why water entrances artists, boys, and ancients alike, Ishmael concludes that the sea's image embodies the elusive, unreachable mystery at the heart of human existence.

children.title: Why a common sailor, not officer
children.gist: He explains he ships as an ordinary sailor rather than a passenger or officer, valuing the pay, the exercise, and the humbling discipline of taking orders.

children.title: Fated to the whaling voyage
children.gist: Ishmael attributes his sudden decision to sail specifically on a whaling voyage to an inscrutable providence that had long been steering him toward this destiny.

children.title: To New Bedford and the Spouter-Inn
children.gist: Arriving in New Bedford before his ship to Nantucket, Ishmael seeks cheap lodging and stumbles into a frightening night sharing a bed with the tattooed harpooneer Queequeg.
children.question: Queequeg the cannibal harpooneer — can a 'savage' prove more honest and humane than civilized men? (a comic trial of prejudice)

children.title: The Carpet-Bag
children.gist: Stranded in New Bedford for a weekend before his Nantucket passage, Ishmael wanders cold streets seeking the cheapest possible inn.

children.title: The Spouter-Inn
children.gist: Ishmael enters the dim, bone-decorated Spouter-Inn and learns he must share a bed with an unseen, allegedly fearsome harpooneer who sells shrunken heads.

children.title: Meeting Queequeg
children.gist: The tattooed cannibal Queequeg returns at night with his idol Yojo, terrifies Ishmael half to death, and then the two reconcile and become fast friends sharing the bed peacefully.

children.title: The Counterpane and morning toilette
children.gist: Waking entangled in Queequeg's tattooed arm, Ishmael reflects on their sudden intimacy and comically observes Queequeg's eccentric but dignified dressing ritual.

children.title: Breakfast among whalemen
children.gist: At the inn's silent, bashful breakfast of weathered whalemen, Queequeg eats coolly with his harpoon, impressing Ishmael with his composure.

children.title: New Bedford, the Chapel, and Father Mapple
children.gist: Ishmael tours New Bedford's whale-funded prosperity, then attends the Whaleman's Chapel where Father Mapple preaches a thundering sermon on Jonah's disobedience and true repentance.
children.question: Jonah's lesson for a pilot of God — what does fleeing one's hard duty cost, and what does real repentance look like? (a sermon with a moral)

children.title: The Street
children.gist: Ishmael marvels at New Bedford's streets, full of cannibal harpooneers and green country boys, and its mansions built entirely on whale-oil wealth.

children.title: The Chapel
children.gist: Visiting the Whaleman's Chapel before sailing, Ishmael reads marble memorial tablets to drowned sailors and reflects on death, grief, and his own strange cheerfulness about mortality.

children.title: Father Mapple's pulpit
children.gist: The renowned ex-harpooneer-turned-preacher Father Mapple climbs his ship-shaped pulpit by a rope ladder which he draws up behind him, symbolizing withdrawal from the world.

children.title: The Sermon on Jonah
children.gist: Father Mapple delivers a thundering sermon retelling Jonah's flight from God's command, his punishment in the whale, and his repentance, drawing the lesson that a true pilot of God must preach truth to falsehood regardless of personal cost.

children.title: Bosom friends bound for Nantucket
children.gist: Ishmael and Queequeg swear eternal friendship, learn Queequeg's royal island backstory, and travel together to Nantucket to find a ship.
children.question: Queequeg's vow of marriage — what does true fellowship look like across the gulf of race and creed? (an intimate bond)

children.title: A Bosom Friend
children.gist: Back at the inn, Ishmael grows fond of Queequeg's calm self-sufficiency, and the two smoke together and solemnly become sworn 'married' friends.

children.title: Worshipping with Queequeg
children.gist: Reasoning that true worship means doing as he would be done by, Ishmael joins Queequeg in his idol worship, and the two share confidences in bed.

children.title: Queequeg's life story
children.gist: Snug under blankets, Queequeg narrates his island royal lineage, his desperate stowaway escape to see Christendom, and his disillusionment with Christian sailors' wickedness.

children.title: Nantucket and signing aboard the Pequod
children.gist: In Nantucket, Ishmael and Queequeg sign onto the Pequod under its shrewd Quaker owners Peleg and Bildad, learning hints of the ship's mysterious, formidable captain Ahab.
children.question: Captain Ahab, unseen — what kind of man commands a ship before he ever appears on deck? (a portrait built from rumor)

children.title: Nantucket, island of whalemen
children.gist: Ishmael praises Nantucket as a barren sand island whose hardy inhabitants nonetheless conquered the world's oceans through whaling.

children.title: Chowder at the Try Pots
children.gist: Settling in at the aptly named Try Pots inn, Ishmael and Queequeg enjoy Mrs. Hussey's excellent chowder amid comic talk of clams and cod.

children.title: Choosing and signing onto the Pequod
children.gist: Guided by Queequeg's idol Yojo, Ishmael selects the strange, bone-decorated ship Pequod and negotiates his pay 'lay' with the voluble co-owner Captain Peleg.

children.title: Bildad and the lays
children.gist: The penny-pinching Quaker owner Bildad haggles over Ishmael's and Queequeg's shares while quoting scripture, revealed as comically mismatched with his hard-driving seafaring past.

children.title: Setting sail under hidden Ahab
children.gist: The Pequod departs Nantucket on Christmas Day commanded in person by the owners, while Ahab remains invisible below, and Ishmael muses on the doomed, landless Bulkington and defends whaling's dignity.
children.question: The Pequod sails without her captain in view — what does it cost a crew to serve a will they cannot yet see? (waiting for a revelation)

children.title: Final preparations and Aunt Charity
children.gist: As the Pequod is provisioned for a three-year voyage, Bildad's sister Aunt Charity fusses over supplies while Ahab remains unseen, said to be recovering below.

children.title: Departure and Bulkington
children.gist: The ship casts off under Peleg and Bildad's command with Ahab still hidden, and Ishmael singles out the restless sailor Bulkington as an emblem of the soul's refusal of safe harbors.

children.title: In defense of whaling's dignity
children.gist: Ishmael mounts a spirited defense of whaling as a noble, history-making vocation unfairly scorned by landsmen, citing historical precedents and economic importance.

children.title: The mates, harpooneers, and Ahab revealed
children.gist: Ishmael profiles the ship's three mates and three harpooneers, then Ahab finally appears on deck, scarred and ivory-legged, and the strange stowaway Fedallah's gang is discovered.
children.question: Ahab's scarred, ivory-legged aspect — what does the captain's body and bearing already tell us about the voyage to come? (a character portrait before the drama)

children.title: Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask
children.gist: Ishmael characterizes the Pequod's three mates: the conscientious, superstitious Starbuck, the easygoing pipe-smoking Stubb, and the pugnacious little Flask.

children.title: Harpooneers and Ahab's first appearance
children.gist: The three pagan harpooneers Queequeg, Tashtego, and Daggoo are introduced, and at last the brooding, ivory-legged Ahab emerges on the quarter-deck in grim majesty.

children.title: Ahab's first clashes with Stubb and his pipe
children.gist: Ahab harshly rebuffs Stubb's mild suggestion about his nightly pacing and then bitterly abandons even the comfort of his pipe, showing his consuming inner torment.

children.title: Fedallah's secret crew revealed
children.gist: At the first whale sighting, Ahab astonishes everyone by unveiling a hidden boat crew led by the sinister Parsee Fedallah, smuggled aboard for his own private purposes.

children.title: Cetology and the quarterdeck oath
children.gist: Ishmael digresses into a full classification of whale species, then Ahab nails a gold doubloon to the mast and extracts a fervent crew oath to hunt and kill Moby Dick.
children.question: The doubloon and the oath — how does Ahab bend an entire crew's will to his single obsession? (a staged ritual of command)

children.title: The Specksnyder and Ahab's command style
children.gist: Ishmael explains the harpooneer officer tradition and how Ahab, though not flaunting rank, exercises an almost sultanic private authority over his officers.

children.title: Cetology: classifying the whales
children.gist: Ishmael undertakes a mock-scholarly bibliographic system sorting all whale species into Folio, Octavo, and Duodecimo 'books' by size, admitting the project can never be complete.

children.title: The mast-head and dreamy philosophers
children.gist: Ishmael describes the solitary, meditative duty of standing mast-head watch and warns that dreamy, Platonist young men risk fatal inattention aloft.

children.title: The Quarter-Deck: Ahab's oath
children.gist: Ahab assembles the crew, nails a gold doubloon to the mast as reward for first sighting Moby Dick, reveals his private vengeance, and binds all but a reluctant Starbuck in a fiery oath to hunt the white whale.

children.title: Night soliloquies: Ahab, Starbuck, Stubb
children.gist: In successive nighttime monologues, Ahab reveals his fatalistic, almost possessed sense of purpose, while Starbuck despairs at his complicity and Stubb resolves to meet it all with reckless humor.

children.title: The history and horror of Moby Dick
children.gist: Ishmael explains the legendary terror surrounding the white whale, his seeming ubiquity and malice, and why his very whiteness strikes deeper dread than any color could.
children.question: Why whiteness terrifies more than blood-red horror — what does the color of nothing reveal about the universe's indifference? (a philosophical digression)

children.title: Forecastle revelry before the storm
children.gist: The international crew sings, dances, and quarrels on the forecastle at night, while the terrified cabin boy Pip cowers as a squall approaches, foreshadowing disaster.

children.title: Moby Dick's fearsome reputation
children.gist: Ishmael recounts how rumor, superstition, and real maimings built Moby Dick's reputation as a uniquely cunning, malicious, nearly supernatural whale that Ahab has come to see as the embodiment of all evil.

children.title: The Whiteness of the Whale
children.gist: Ishmael argues at length that it is specifically the whale's ghastly whiteness, evoking blankness and soulless dread rather than any single horror, that makes him so uniquely appalling to the imagination.

children.title: Omens: Elijah's return and the chart
children.gist: Overheard rumors below decks, a chase after a giant squid mistaken for the whale, and Ahab's obsessive chart-work all deepen the sense of a voyage shadowed by fate.

children.title: Proofs, portents, and Ahab's hidden madness
children.gist: Ishmael marshals real-world testimony that whales can sink ships, then traces how Ahab's leg wound curdled into a monomania that cunningly conceals its full derangement from the world.
children.question: Ahab's 'monomania' — can a man be mad in one single idea and yet brilliantly, terribly sane in everything else? (a psychological case)

children.title: The Affidavit: whales really do sink ships
children.gist: Ishmael cites documented cases, including the Essex disaster, to establish that sperm whales have genuinely and deliberately destroyed large ships, lending credibility to Moby Dick's story.

children.title: Surmises: keeping the crew's eyes on profit too
children.gist: Ishmael explains Ahab's calculated strategy of still pursuing ordinary whales to keep his crew financially invested and distracted from dwelling on the uncanny main quest.

children.title: The Mat-Maker and first lowering
children.gist: While musing on fate, chance, and free will while weaving a mat with Queequeg, Ishmael is interrupted by the cry of whales sighted, triggering the first dramatic chase that reveals Fedallah's crew.

children.title: First chases: squall, shark massacre, cutting-in
children.gist: The crew survives a terrifying squall after a first failed lowering, then kills and processes their first whale aboard the Pequod amid sharks, blubber, and grim camaraderie.
children.question: The whale's carcass as mirror — what do the brutal, intimate labors of butchering a whale reveal about the men who do it? (a shipboard apprenticeship)

children.title: The Hyena: surviving the squall
children.gist: After the terrifying first lowering ends in a capsized boat and a night adrift in a squall, Ishmael reflects wryly on fear, fate, and resolves his will before danger.

children.title: Fedallah's boat and crew explained
children.gist: Ishmael details how Ahab secretly recruited Fedallah and his exotic boat crew, and the superstitious crew's uneasy fascination with the enigmatic Parsee.

children.title: Stubb kills a whale
children.gist: Stubb coolly and skillfully kills the Pequod's first whale of the voyage while smoking his pipe, demonstrating veteran whalecraft and his characteristic humor under danger.

children.title: Stubb's supper and whale cuisine
children.gist: Stubb demands a whale steak and comically lectures the ship's black cook Fleece on sermonizing to the sharks, while Ishmael surveys the surprising culinary and cultural uses of whale flesh.

children.title: The Town-Ho's story and whaling's human cost
children.gist: A visiting ship's tale of mutiny and supernatural retribution involving Moby Dick is recounted, bracketed by scenes of Pip's abandonment at sea and the grim toil of working the ship.
children.question: Steelkilt's mutiny and Pip's abandonment — what happens to the powerless when captains and crews pursue their own ends? (two tales of the overlooked)

children.title: The Town-Ho's Story
children.gist: Ishmael narrates, as told later in Lima, how a sailor's mutiny against a brutal mate aboard the Town-Ho was followed by Moby Dick's sudden, fatal intervention that seemed to deliver poetic justice.

children.title: Monstrous and true pictures of whales
children.gist: Ishmael surveys centuries of wildly inaccurate artistic and scientific depictions of whales, arguing the living leviathan's true form can never be adequately captured in any picture.

children.title: Brit, squid, and the ocean's malice
children.gist: Sailing through fields of whale food and sighting an ominous giant squid, Ishmael meditates on the sea's universal cannibalism and its treacherous indifference to human life.

children.title: The whale-line's deadly intimacy
children.gist: Ishmael describes the coiled whale-line's beauty and horror, how it entangles the boat crew in constant mortal danger, and uses it as a metaphor for life's ever-present unseen perils.

children.title: Pip's abandonment at sea
children.gist: After twice leaping from Stubb's boat in panic, the small cabin boy Pip is left behind in the vast ocean and, though eventually rescued, emerges apparently insane, his soul touched by cosmic vastness.

children.title: A Squeeze of the Hand and whale-processing
children.gist: Ishmael rhapsodizes on the sensual, companionable pleasure of squeezing spermaceti lumps with shipmates, then catalogs the many odd products and labors of processing whale blubber.

children.title: Try-works, omens, and the doubloon's many readings
children.gist: The ship's try-works burn through the night like a hell-ship, Ahab shatters his quadrant for its false guidance, and each crew member reads his own fate in the mast-head gold coin.
children.question: The doubloon as mirror — does the coin reveal each man's fate, or only the self he brings to read it? (a parable of interpretation)

children.title: The Try-Works: hell-ship by night
children.gist: Ishmael describes the terrifying, infernal spectacle of the ship's try-works burning at night, during which he nearly steers the ship to disaster after a trance-like vision of darkness.

children.title: Stowing down and clearing up
children.gist: After oil is cooled and stored, the ship is scrubbed spotless, only for lookouts to spy more whales, renewing the exhausting cycle of labor that Ishmael likens to life's endless repetition.

children.title: The Doubloon: each man reads his own fate
children.gist: Ahab, Starbuck, Stubb, Flask, the old Manxman, Queequeg, Fedallah, and the mad Pip each interpret the zodiac-stamped gold doubloon nailed to the mast according to his own character and obsessions.

children.title: Leg and Arm: the Samuel Enderby
children.gist: The Pequod meets the English whaler Samuel Enderby, whose good-humored one-armed captain also lost a limb to Moby Dick but, unlike Ahab, sensibly wants nothing more to do with him.

children.title: The Decanter: English whaling hospitality
children.gist: Ishmael praises the generous, high-living hospitality of English whaling ships, tracing its roots to old Dutch whaling customs of abundant food and drink.

children.title: Ahab's leg, the carpenter, and Starbuck's confrontation
children.gist: After his ivory leg is damaged, Ahab has a new one forged while musing darkly on fate and suffering, nearly provokes mutiny over a leak, and Starbuck wavers on the edge of killing him.
children.question: Starbuck's musket at the cabin door — what stays the hand of the one man who could end the voyage by violence? (a moral crisis)

children.title: Ahab's leg and the forging of the new harpoon
children.gist: After his ivory leg is damaged, Ahab orders both a replacement leg and a special new harpoon, tempered in the blood of his harpooneers, intended solely for Moby Dick.

children.title: Ahab and the Carpenter's dialogue
children.gist: In a strange philosophical exchange, Ahab needles the literal-minded ship's carpenter about pain, identity, and mortality while his new ivory leg is being made.

children.title: Starbuck's confrontation over the leak
children.gist: Starbuck openly challenges Ahab's refusal to address a dangerous oil leak, and Ahab, after nearly threatening him with a musket, relents and orders the leak checked.

children.title: Queequeg's coffin and recovery
children.gist: Gravely ill, Queequeg has a coffin built to his specifications in native style, then unexpectedly recovers by willing himself to live, later repurposing the coffin as a sea-chest.

children.title: Into the Pacific: gilder calms and the Bachelor
children.gist: The Pequod enters the Pacific's deceptive tranquility, Ahab's rare tender moment with Starbuck is undercut by his fatalism, and a lucky, oblivious whaler named the Bachelor passes by.
children.question: Ahab's one tender confession to Starbuck — can a moment of human feeling turn aside a will already surrendered to fate? (a near-reprieve)

children.title: The Pacific and the Gilder's deceptive calm
children.gist: Entering the vast Pacific intensifies Ahab's purpose, while the serene 'Gilder' seas tempt Ahab, Starbuck, and Stubb into brief, contrasting daydreams of peace before the final hunt.

children.title: The Blacksmith's ruined life
children.gist: Ishmael tells the sorrowful backstory of the ship's blacksmith Perth, whose family and prosperity were destroyed by drink, leading him to seek oblivion in whaling.

children.title: Ahab's confession to Starbuck
children.gist: Gazing at a dying whale and in a rare unguarded moment, Ahab confesses to Starbuck the forty wasted years of his life and nearly relents toward home, before fatalism reclaims him.

children.title: The typhoon and corpusants
children.gist: A violent typhoon strikes the ship; Ahab defies the lightning-charmed masts and inverted compass with blasphemous resolve, while Starbuck is tempted toward mutiny or murder.
children.question: Fire from heaven on the masts — does Ahab's defiance of the storm's omens prove his supremacy, or only his damnation? (a battle of wills with nature)

children.title: The Dying Whale and the Whale Watch
children.gist: Watching a freshly killed whale die facing the sun, Ahab draws dark lessons about faith and fate, while that night the Parsee Fedallah delivers his cryptic prophecy about hearses and Ahab's immortality.

children.title: The Typhoon strikes
children.gist: A violent typhoon battering the ship culminates in corpusant flames crowning the masts, which Ahab defiantly embraces as a sign of his fiery kinship rather than fearing as divine warning.

children.title: Starbuck's temptation with the musket
children.gist: Alone at night with a loaded musket outside Ahab's cabin, Starbuck wrestles with the temptation to kill his captain to save the ship, but ultimately cannot bring himself to do it.

children.title: The Rachel, the coffin life-buoy, and Ahab's hat
children.gist: A grieving captain begs Ahab's help finding his lost son, Ahab refuses, and ominous signs multiply: a repurposed coffin life-buoy, a lost hat, and a ship named Delight burying its dead.
children.question: Ahab's refusal of the Rachel's plea — what does a father's weeping request reveal about what Ahab has already sacrificed? (a test of remaining humanity)

children.title: Pip in the cabin, Ahab's hat lost
children.gist: Ahab takes the deranged Pip into his own cabin in a gesture of strange tenderness, while a wild hawk seizes Ahab's hat and drops it into the sea, an omen the crew cannot ignore.

children.title: The Pequod meets the Delight
children.gist: The battered whaler Delight, having just lost five men to Moby Dick and about to bury them at sea, warns Ahab that no harpoon forged can kill the white whale.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 131. The Pequod Meets The Delight.

children.title: The Symphony: Ahab's last confession
children.gist: In a moment of serene weather, Ahab tearfully confesses his wasted life to Starbuck and seems to waver toward turning home, but a glimpse of Fedallah's reflection snuffs out the impulse.

children.title: The three-day chase and the final destruction
children.gist: Over three days Ahab pursues Moby Dick, losing his boat, his harpooneer Fedallah, and finally his ship and his life, as the whale sinks the Pequod and all but Ishmael perish.
children.question: The three-day chase — when it finally comes, does confronting Moby Dick bring Ahab anything but total annihilation? (the catastrophe arrives)

children.title: First Day: the whale's jaws close
children.gist: Ahab's boat is destroyed in the first encounter with Moby Dick, and Ahab, though gravely endangered, vows to resume the hunt immediately with unbroken resolve.

children.title: Second Day: three boats smashed, Fedallah lost
children.gist: A renewed assault leaves three boats wrecked and the Parsee Fedallah missing, fulfilling half his own ominous prophecy, while Ahab's fury only intensifies toward a third and final day.

children.title: Third Day: the Pequod sinks
children.gist: On the third day Moby Dick kills Fedallah's lashed corpse is seen on his back, rams and sinks the Pequod itself, and drags Ahab down with him, destroying the ship and all its crew but one.

children.title: Epilogue: Ishmael alone survives
children.gist: Ishmael alone survives the wreck, kept afloat by Queequeg's coffin-turned-life-buoy, until the grieving Rachel, still searching for her own lost children, rescues him.
